name: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain?

positions.claim: Britain's labour was dear and its coal cheap, so machines that swapped coal and capital for labour paid there first.
positions.mech: Relative factor prices steer invention: the jenny, the water frame and the steam engine were profitable in Britain and not in France or India.
for: London wages bought more silver and food than wages in Paris, Vienna, Delhi or Beijing.
Coal at the pithead in Newcastle was among the cheapest energy in the world.
Allen's returns on early machines are high in England and low elsewhere.
against: Humphries: the machines replaced women's and children's labour, which was cheap.
Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda: high wages reflect productive workers, not cost pressure.
The Dutch had high wages too and no industrial revolution.

positions.claim: An Enlightenment culture of useful knowledge, linking natural philosophers and craftsmen, made British invention cumulative.
positions.mech: Societies, journals and lectures cut the cost of access to knowledge, so one improvement built on the next.
for: Dense networks such as the Lunar Society tied savants to makers.
Patents and inventors cluster where the institutions of open science were strongest.
against: The Enlightenment was European; France had more formal science.
The effect of culture is hard to measure.

positions.claim: Britain escaped the land constraint that also bound the Yangzi delta thanks to coal close to markets and New World land and slave labour.
positions.mech: Coal replaced wood and muscle (the organic economy); American cotton, sugar and timber were ghost acres Britain did not have to farm.
for: Coal supplied energy equal to millions of acres of woodland.
Raw cotton came from the Americas.
Atlantic markets bought British manufactures.
against: Broadberry et al. find England already richer than the Yangzi delta before 1700.
China also had coal, though far from its core.

positions.claim: Britain's edge was a deep pool of skilled mechanics and healthy workers who could build, run and improve machines.
positions.mech: Invention needs implementation: millwrights, clockmakers and smiths turned prototypes into factories.
for: Mechanisation spread fastest where mechanics were already plentiful.
British workers were taller and better fed than French ones.
against: English literacy stagnated in 1750-1850.
Skills are measured indirectly.

positions.claim: Centuries in which the rich left more surviving children spread middle-class habits through the English population.
positions.mech: Downward social mobility carried literacy, thrift and work discipline into the mass of the population.
for: Wills show richer men left more surviving children.
Interest rates fell and literacy rose before 1800.
against: How such traits would pass down is speculative.
Similar fertility patterns existed in China and Japan without industrialisation.

state: Most economic historians now combine cheap coal and relative prices with Mokyr's knowledge and a skills story; the live fight is whether high wages pushed firms to mechanise or simply showed that British workers were productive. Clark's selection argument has few followers.
settle: Firm-level costs of adopting early machines in Britain, France and India using wages for women and children, and evidence on where inventors and mechanics came from and what they knew.
fun: Was the steam engine invented because English workers cost too much, or because English tinkerers knew too much?

name: When did Western Europe actually start to become rich?

positions.claim: England and Holland pulled ahead from the late fourteenth century and never fell back; the North Sea was richer than most of the world by 1500-1700.
positions.mech: Post-plague gains in output per head were kept, then compounded by trade and structural change.
for: Reconstructed English GDP per head rises after 1348 and again after 1650.
Holland's income per head was the world's highest by about 1600.
against: Day wages in England fell back in the sixteenth century.
Asian national accounts before 1800 are thin.

positions.claim: The Black Death lifted wages, and the urbanisation and wars it financed kept death rates high enough to hold incomes up.
positions.mech: A Malthusian model with a one-off shock: higher incomes bought towns and armies, both of which killed people, so incomes stayed high.
for: Urbanisation and war frequency rose after 1350.
The model reproduces the European income path.
against: It explains a high-income equilibrium, not growth.
China also had wars and epidemics.

positions.claim: The richest parts of China and India matched England until about 1750-1800; Western riches are recent and owe much to coal and empire.
positions.mech: Similar Smithian market economies everywhere met the same ecological limits; Britain broke them by luck and force.
for: Life expectancy and consumption in the Yangzi delta compare well with England.
Indian cotton cloth led the world into the eighteenth century.
against: Wage and GDP series show Asia behind by 1600-1700 (Broadberry and Gupta; Allen).

positions.claim: Before the Industrial Revolution living standards everywhere hovered near subsistence; sustained riches begin only after 1800.
positions.mech: Any income gain raised population until incomes fell back.
for: Real wages show no sustained trend before 1800.
Growth of over 1 percent a year per head appears only in the nineteenth century.
against: Reconstructed national accounts show England and Holland well above subsistence by 1700.

positions.claim: Households in north-west Europe got richer from the mid-seventeenth century by working more days for the market, not by higher day wages.
positions.mech: A taste for new goods (sugar, tea, cloth) drew labour into the market; annual earnings rose as days worked rose.
for: Annual earnings series rise while day wages stagnate.
Probate inventories fill with new consumer goods.
against: Working more is not the same as getting richer per hour.

state: The numbers now give Rishi two answers. North-west Europe, England and Holland first, was richer than most of the world by 1500-1700, after the Black Death. Rich in the modern sense, with income per head growing more than 1 percent a year for generations, began only after about 1800 with the Industrial Revolution.
settle: Better Asian national accounts before 1800 and family-level real incomes (including women's work) for Europe and Asia.
fun: The Black Death may have done more for Western European living standards than any king: the question is whether the gains stuck.

name: What caused the French Revolution?

positions.claim: A rising capitalist bourgeoisie overthrew a feudal aristocracy, with peasant and urban popular revolutions running alongside.
positions.mech: Class conflict produced by economic change; Lefebvre saw four revolutions in 1789: aristocratic, bourgeois, popular and peasant.
for: Peasant risings forced the abolition of feudalism.
The Revolution ended legal privilege.
against: The revolutionaries were mostly lawyers and office-holders, not capitalists (Cobban).
Nobles and bourgeois often shared investments and ideas.

positions.claim: No capitalist class made the Revolution; its dynamic came from politics and the language of popular sovereignty.
positions.mech: Once the king lost authority, competing claims to speak for the nation drove radicalisation.
for: Social profiles of deputies.
Radical rhetoric ran ahead of social interests.
against: Underplays bread, hunger and fiscal facts.

positions.school: Bankruptcy and the politics of consent
positions.claim: War debt bankrupted the monarchy; without an institution to commit to taxes it had to summon the Estates-General and lost control.
positions.mech: Debt service consumed a huge share of revenue; reform needed consent the privileged would not give.
for: Calonne admitted the deficit in 1786; the treasury suspended payments in August 1788.
Britain, with Parliament, borrowed more cheaply.
against: Explains why 1789 came but not why it went so far.

positions.claim: Drought, the hailstorm of 13 July 1788 and a hard winter wrecked the harvest; dear bread put crowds on the streets in 1789.
positions.mech: Harvest failure doubled grain prices and cut demand for manufactures, so the poor lost income as bread rose.
for: The Paris loaf peaked on 14 July 1789.
The Réveillon riot, the Bastille, the Great Fear and the October Days all tied to bread.
against: Bad harvests had come before without revolution.
Weather was a trigger, not a cause.

positions.claim: The eighteenth-century commercial boom did create a confident middle class and public sphere that demanded a voice: a social interpretation without Marxist class.
positions.mech: Consumption, print and professions built a public that judged the crown.
for: Growth of trade, newspapers and professional bodies.
against: Hard to show this class acted as one in 1789.

state: Political and fiscal breakdown opened the door; a weather-driven bread crisis brought crowds through it. The 1950s Marxist class model is abandoned, but social history has returned in Jones and others.
settle: Commune-level series of prices, riots and weather; comparisons with other fiscal crises with and without harvest failure.
fun: A hailstorm on 13 July 1788 flattened crops across northern France; a year and a day later Paris stormed the Bastille with bread at its peak price.

name: Why did a million people die in the Irish famine?

positions.school: Ecological shock on a poor economy
positions.claim: An unprecedented blight hit a society where the poorest third lived on potatoes alone; poverty, not overpopulation, made it lethal.
positions.mech: Phytophthora destroyed the one food the poor had, for four years out of five.
for: Blight took about a third of the 1845 crop and three-quarters in 1846.
Mokyr finds no link between population density and deaths across counties.
against: Belgium and the Netherlands lost potatoes too, with far fewer deaths.

positions.claim: Relief shaped by laissez-faire and providentialism, and then dumped on Irish poor rates, turned crop failure into mass death.
positions.mech: Public works paid too little, soup kitchens were closed early, and the Gregory clause made land the price of food.
for: Soup kitchens fed 3 million a day in 1847 and cut mortality, then were closed.
Trevelyan called the famine Providence's remedy.
against: Even generous relief could not have replaced the potato entirely (Ó Gráda).

positions.claim: Population growth on the potato pushed Ireland past what it could feed, and a check was coming.
positions.mech: Early marriage on cheap potato land drove growth until subsistence failed.
for: Population reached 8.2 million in 1841.
against: Mokyr: densely settled counties did not suffer more.
Population growth had already slowed before 1845.

positions.claim: British policy was deliberate enough to meet the legal definition of genocide.
positions.mech: Officials knew relief cuts would kill and chose them to remake Irish land.
for: Exports and evictions continued while people starved.
against: Specialists find neglect and ideology, not intent to destroy.
Britain spent about 7 million pounds on relief.

state: Historians agree blight was the trigger and policy the multiplier; they argue over the weight. Culpable neglect is mainstream; genocide is rejected by most specialists.
settle: Poor-law-union mortality matched to relief spending; comparison with blight years in Belgium, the Netherlands and the Highlands.
fun: Blight hit Belgium, the Netherlands and the Scottish Highlands too; only in Ireland did a million die.

name: Were the famines of 1876-79 acts of nature or of policy?

positions.claim: El Niño droughts struck societies that colonial rule and world markets had made fragile; policy turned drought into mass death.
positions.mech: Laissez-faire relief, exports and the loss of older safety nets.
for: Grain left famine districts.
Temple's one-pound ration on relief works.
against: Calling them holocausts implies an intent most historians do not find.
China, not a colony, suffered as badly.

positions.claim: Ideas about dependency made Indian relief deliberately harsh in 1876-78; the scandal produced the Famine Codes.
positions.mech: Officials set tests and rations to deter, not to save.
for: Bombay and Madras relief records.
The 1880 Famine Commission.
against: Policy improved quickly afterwards.

positions.claim: In north China the decay of granaries and state capacity after the mid-century rebellions explains the scale of death.
positions.mech: Without full granaries and transport, relief came late to landlocked Shanxi.
for: Eighteenth-century relief worked in similar droughts.
against: Climate shock was exceptional.

positions.claim: Rail links let grain flow into drought districts, so famines grew less deadly over time.
positions.mech: Market integration spreads a local shortfall across a wider area.
for: Rail-linked districts show smaller price and mortality responses to rainfall.
against: Davis: railways also carried grain away from the hungry.

state: Few dispute that the 1876-78 droughts were linked to El Niño and that policy multiplied death in India; the debate is about intent, the role of markets, and the Chinese state.
settle: District-level mortality matched to relief spending, exports and rail access; Chinese gazetteer data on granaries.
fun: The same warm Pacific dried fields in Madras, Shanxi and Ceará in the same two years: how many deaths came from the sky?

name: Who started the First World War?

positions.claim: Germany's leaders sought or accepted a continental war in 1914 to break encirclement and win hegemony.
positions.mech: The blank cheque pushed Austria on, knowing Russia might fight.
for: The September 1914 war-aims programme.
German military leaders wanted war before Russian rearmament ended.
against: The September programme came after the war began.
Long premeditation since 1912 is not proven.

positions.claim: Decision-makers in every capital, Belgrade and St Petersburg included, chose risk; no single culprit.
positions.mech: Fragmented governments, alliance commitments and short-term thinking.
for: Serbian nationalist networks.
Franco-Russian coordination during Poincaré's July visit.
against: Underplays Berlin and Vienna's deliberate choices (Mombauer).

positions.claim: Russia's ambitions at the Straits and early secret mobilisation turned a Balkan war into a general one.
positions.mech: Pre-mobilisation from 25-26 July forced Germany's hand.
for: Russian military measures began before Austria mobilised against Russia.
against: Russian aims at the Straits did not need war in 1914.

positions.claim: Austria-Hungary chose war with Serbia for its own survival; Berlin enabled rather than drove it.
positions.mech: Fear of South Slav nationalism after the Balkan Wars.
for: Vienna's ministers decided for war in early July.
against: Without Berlin, Vienna would not have dared.

positions.claim: Alliances, militarism, the naval race and mobilisation plans made war likely once a crisis came.
positions.mech: Rigid plans and blocs left little time for diplomacy.
for: Mobilisation meant war in German planning.
The naval race pushed Britain toward the Entente.
against: Earlier crises (1905, 1911, 1912-13) did not end in war.

state: Since 2012 the field is split between Clark's distributed responsibility and those, such as Mombauer, who still put most weight on Berlin and Vienna. Few accept Fischer's long premeditation; most accept that Berlin and Vienna chose risk deliberately in July.
settle: Russian records on the period preparatory to war; Austrian and German decision papers of early July.
fun: Five capitals, 37 days: Clark says everyone sleepwalked, Fischer said Berlin was wide awake.

name: What caused the Great Depression?

positions.claim: The Fed let banking panics shrink the money stock by about a third, turning a recession into the Great Contraction.
positions.mech: Money fell as people and banks hoarded cash; the Fed did not offset it.
for: M2 fell about a third from 1929 to 1933.
Recovery followed monetary expansion after 1933.
against: Why the panics, and why abroad too?

positions.claim: The restored gold standard spread deflation worldwide and stopped any country acting alone.
positions.mech: Gold flows forced tightening; leaving gold freed policy.
for: Countries recovered in the order they left gold.
Fed tightening of 1928 drained gold from Europe.
against: The US held plenty of gold and could have expanded.

positions.claim: A fall in consumer spending in 1930, partly from post-crash uncertainty, started the slide before money contracted.
positions.mech: Durable purchases collapsed.
for: Consumption fell more than income in 1930.
against: Monetary contraction did most of the damage after 1930.

positions.claim: Bank failures destroyed lending relationships and choked credit beyond the money effect.
positions.mech: Information about borrowers died with the banks.
for: Output tracks failures and deposits lost, not only money.
against: Hard to separate from monetary effects.

positions.claim: Britain could no longer and the United States would not yet stabilise the world economy: no lender of last resort, no open market.
positions.mech: Without a hegemon, beggar-thy-neighbour policies spread.
for: Reparations tangle; Smoot-Hawley; failure of the 1933 London conference.
against: Irwin: tariffs did little to output.

state: The consensus synthesis is monetary contraction under the gold standard, made worse by banking collapse (Bernanke shared the 2022 Nobel prize for that work). Spending and hegemony stories survive as parts; Smoot-Hawley is seen as minor for output.
settle: Better cross-country data on bank failures, credit and output, and on the timing of policy shifts.
fun: Countries that left gold early recovered early: Britain bounced from 1932, the gold bloc sank until 1935-36.

name: How and when was the Holocaust decided?

positions.claim: Hitler intended to destroy the Jews long before the war and carried it out step by step.
positions.mech: Ideology drove policy from the top.
for: Hitler's 1939 'prophecy'.
Antisemitism at the core of Nazi ideology.
against: Policy shifted from emigration to deportation schemes before murder.
No written order exists.

positions.claim: Rival agencies in a chaotic regime radicalised policy step by step; failed territorial solutions led to improvised murder.
positions.mech: Bureaucratic process and competition, with Hitler setting goals vaguely.
for: Madagascar and Lublin plans.
Hilberg's sequence of definition, expropriation, concentration and annihilation.
against: Underplays Hitler's role and ideology.

positions.claim: Hitler's ideology set the direction; the decision emerged in stages between summer 1941 and spring 1942.
positions.mech: Officials anticipated Hitler's wishes; victory euphoria (Browning, October 1941) or war with the US (Gerlach, December 1941) marked the turn.
for: Escalation of shootings from August 1941.
Goebbels's diary on Hitler's speech of 12 December 1941.
against: Dating the decision still divides its proponents.

positions.claim: A widespread German eliminationist antisemitism made ordinary Germans willing executioners.
positions.mech: Belief, not pressure, explains the killers.
for: Perpetrators often killed with zeal and cruelty.
against: Browning: the same men shot from conformity; non-German auxiliaries killed too.

positions.claim: The killing happened where Soviet and Nazi power overlapped and destroyed states, tied to plans to starve the east.
positions.mech: Statelessness removed every protection.
for: Most victims lived in the zone between Berlin and Moscow.
The Hunger Plan.
against: Treats Soviet and Nazi killing in one frame, which critics reject.

state: The intentionalist-functionalist split has given way to a synthesis: Hitler's ideology mattered, decisions came in stages in 1941-42, and many agencies and ordinary men took part. Goldhagen's thesis is largely rejected; the exact date of the decision is still argued.
settle: Further Soviet-area archives and perpetrator records; any document dating the decision.
fun: No written order has been found; historians date the decision anywhere from July 1941 to spring 1942.

name: Who started the Cold War?

positions.claim: Soviet ideology and expansion in eastern Europe forced a reluctant United States to respond.
positions.mech: Stalin broke wartime promises; the West contained him.
for: Broken Yalta promises in Poland.
Pressure on Iran, Turkey and Greece.
against: Ignores American power and interests.

positions.claim: American economic expansion and atomic diplomacy provoked Soviet defensiveness.
positions.mech: The US demanded open markets and used the bomb as leverage.
for: Marshall aid tied to open trade.
Timing of the atomic bombings.
against: Soviet archives show Stalin's own expansive aims.

positions.claim: Both sides misread each other; later, with Soviet archives, Gaddis put the main weight on Stalin.
positions.mech: Security dilemma plus Stalin's personality.
for: Long Telegram to Truman Doctrine.
Soviet documents opened after 1991.
against: Shifts between balance and blame.

positions.claim: US leaders, fearing Soviet gains from chaos, sought a preponderance of power that Moscow read as encirclement.
positions.mech: Reasonable fears produced escalating actions.
for: Policy papers of the Truman administration.
against: Gives less weight to Soviet ideology.

positions.claim: Two universal ideologies fought to shape the modern world, above all in the decolonising Third World.
positions.mech: Ideology and security fused; the South became the main battlefield.
for: Soviet and Chinese archives.
Interventions from Korea to Afghanistan.
against: Explains the war's spread more than its 1945-47 start.

state: Since the Soviet archives opened, most historians give Stalin heavy responsibility but frame the conflict as ideological and global, with American security fears and power also driving escalation. Pure revisionism is a minority view.
settle: Fuller Russian archives on Stalin's aims in 1945-48.
fun: Kennan's long telegram from Moscow became the blueprint of containment: was he describing Soviet insecurity or creating American fear?

name: Why did the Soviet Union collapse in 1991?

positions.claim: The system fell because its own leaders, believers in reform, dismantled the party's powers and elites took the assets.
positions.mech: Reform from above destroyed the glue of the system.
for: No army or KGB defended the Union in December 1991.
against: Explains why it fell quietly more than why it fell.

positions.claim: Gorbachev's choices, above all political liberalisation, not structural decline, made the end possible.
positions.mech: Leadership determines whether a stagnant system reforms, persists or breaks.
for: The USSR in 1985 was stagnant but stable.
against: Underplays fiscal and national pressures.

positions.claim: Gorbachev's economic reforms failed because entrenched lobbies blocked price reform while deficits soared; China managed what Moscow could not.
positions.mech: Interest groups and a budget hole.
for: Anti-alcohol campaign cut revenue.
Enterprise reform raised wages without prices.
against: Political dissolution came from nationalism too.

positions.claim: Dependence on oil exports to pay for grain imports doomed the USSR when oil prices collapsed in 1986.
positions.mech: Loss of hard currency, then of credit.
for: Oil price roughly halved in 1986.
Grain imports had grown since the 1960s.
against: Other petro-states survived the same price fall.

positions.claim: Nationalist mobilisation, and finally Ukraine's vote for independence, ended the Union.
positions.mech: Glasnost let a tide of national movements rise; without Ukraine Russia would not stay.
for: Over 90 percent voted for Ukrainian independence on 1 December 1991.
against: Russia itself, under Yeltsin, also left.

state: Few now think the USSR had to fall when it did; most combine Gorbachev's political choices, a self-inflicted fiscal crisis and nationalist mobilisation, with oil as aggravation.
settle: Republic-level budget and Party archives for 1988-91.
fun: Superpowers usually die in wars; this one was dissolved by signatures in a hunting lodge in Belarus.

name: Why was India partitioned, and why so violently?

positions.claim: Pakistan was a bargaining counter for Muslim parity at the centre; Congress's insistence on a strong centre made partition the result.
positions.mech: High politics among Jinnah, Congress and the British.
for: Jinnah accepted the Cabinet Mission Plan for a united India.
against: Dhulipala: Pakistan was a popular, concrete idea, not just a tactic.

positions.claim: Pakistan was widely discussed and wanted as a sovereign Islamic state, a "new Medina".
positions.mech: Ulama and League propaganda built mass support.
for: United Provinces press and pamphlets, 1940-47.
against: Concentrates on a province that did not become Pakistan.

positions.claim: A Britain weakened by war left fast, with no plan to protect people, and the state collapsed into violence.
positions.mech: The 1947 deadline outran planning and security.
for: Ten weeks from plan to independence.
Boundaries published after independence.
against: Indian actors drove the demand for partition.

positions.claim: Bengal Hindu elites demanded partition of their province to escape Muslim-majority rule.
positions.mech: Partition was sought from below by Hindus too, not only by the League.
for: 1947 petitions and campaigns for West Bengal.
against: A regional dynamic, not the all-India story.

positions.claim: Organised local violence did not follow partition, it made it: militias cleansed territory and fixed identities.
positions.mech: Reprisal chains and armed bands.
for: From Calcutta to Noakhali to Bihar to Punjab.
against: Explains the violence more than the decision.

state: The field has moved from high politics (Jalal) to a mix of popular politics, regional demands and the collapse of order as Britain withdrew. Most agree the speed of the 1947 handover multiplied the violence.
settle: Local studies of how violence was organised; more on Pakistan's popular appeal outside the United Provinces.
fun: The border was published two days after independence: millions learned which country they were in after it existed.
